archetype.name: Playoff Team (run-first, QB-dependent)
archetype.definition: A team whose play backs up its record, built on Derrick Henry's volume and a very efficient passing game, with a middling defense and a ceiling set almost entirely by whether Lamar Jackson is on the field.

report.headline: A top-five team by efficiency, but only as good as Lamar's ankle
report.take:
The first Ravens team under Jesse Minter is a ground-and-pound offense with a sharp passing game attached. They rank 5th in net EPA and 7th in offensive EPA, score 26 points a game, and lean on the run more than almost anyone (pass rate over expected -4.7, 26th). Henry has 130 carries and the line has the run game at 4.61 yards a carry, 4th in the league. The 4-2 record is honest: wins over expected sits at 0.2, against last year's -2.8, when an 8-9 team kept losing close games it could have won. This version isn't living on luck in either direction.

The engine is the passing efficiency when Jackson plays. The offense is 6th in pass EPA, and his four starts produced passing EPA of 10.3, 3.3, 11.9 and 12 in the box scores. That efficiency is what makes the heavy run rate work: defenses can't sell out on Henry. The defense gives back a lot of that edge. It ranks 16th in EPA allowed, 24th in pressure rate and 22nd in takeaways, so it rarely ends drives on its own. It is good underneath (4th in short-pass EPA allowed) and poor deep (22nd), and opposing No. 1 receivers have done more against it than against almost any other defense (0.64 EPA a play, 31st).

The season splits in two. With Tyler Huntley, Atlanta was won on the ground, with 208 rushing yards and a rush EPA of 7.3, and Cleveland was lost when the run died (rush EPA of -10) in a 13-10 game. A Huntley offense has to run well to win; a Jackson offense doesn't. The self-inflicted damage runs through both halves: 8.3 penalties a game (26th), 4.2 of them on the line (27th), special teams at -1.44 EPA a game (23rd), and a 31st-ranked short-yardage conversion rate on a team that goes for it on fourth down more than anyone. That costs points a team this efficient shouldn't be giving away.

The AFC North is a three-way tie at 4-2 with Cincinnati a half-game back, and the next stretch decides a lot: the Bengals at home, then Buffalo's top-ranked offense on the road. Jackson is day-to-day and could practice this week, and center Cam Jurgens, a 100% snap player, is out with a concussion. If Jackson comes back near full strength, this is a division favorite with a top-ten offense. If he doesn't, it's a run-reliant team with a league-average defense in a division where every game is close.

strengths.title: Elite passing efficiency with Jackson
strengths.body: The pass offense ranks 6th in EPA a play even with the league's 26th-ranked pass rate over expected, so the Ravens throw less but get a lot out of each attempt. Jackson's starts carried most of that, with double-digit passing EPA in three of them. The efficiency holds as long as he is healthy, which is the open question.

strengths.title: Henry and a line that moves people
strengths.body: Henry's 130 carries anchor an offense averaging 4.61 yards a carry (4th) with a 43.1% run success rate (9th). The run game kept producing through the QB change, with 208 rushing yards at Atlanta. It's built on volume and line play rather than game script, so it should last, though Jurgens' absence tests it.

strengths.title: Tight underneath pass defense
strengths.body: The defense allows little on short throws (4th in short-pass EPA) and holds lead tight ends in check (5th in EPA a play to TE1s). Quick-game offenses have trouble moving it methodically. That makes the deep ball and No. 1 receivers the main ways teams beat it.

concerns.title: The offense shrinks without Jackson
concerns.body: Huntley's two starts left the offense dependent on the run. When Henry was stuffed in Cleveland, passing EPA of 4.6 couldn't make up for a -10 rush EPA and the team scored 10 points. Sacks also climbed in his starts. This is the biggest variable in the season, and the ankle is day-to-day rather than resolved.

concerns.title: A defense that doesn't take the ball
concerns.body: A 24th-ranked pressure rate and 6 takeaways (22nd) mean the defense rarely creates short fields or ends drives early. It also leaks on deep throws (22nd in deep EPA allowed). This looks structural rather than unlucky, with a QB hit rate that ranks 9th but isn't turning into sacks or turnovers.

concerns.title: Penalties, special teams, short yardage
concerns.body: A good offense keeps stalling itself: 8.3 penalties a game, 131 penalty yards in a Week 4 win that didn't cover, below-average special teams and the 31st-ranked short-yardage rate. Paired with a coach who goes for it on every fourth down that qualifies, poor short-yardage play turns aggression into handing the ball over on downs. These are fixable, but they show up every week.

trend.note: The offense ran hot through Jackson's four starts apart from the New Orleans upset. With Huntley it swung from a 208-yard rushing win at Atlanta to a 10-point loss in Cleveland. The defense has been steady and unspectacular throughout.

nextGame.headline: Henry against a leaky run defense, if the pocket holds
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati is close to a mirror image: 7th in net EPA to Baltimore's 5th, and the most pass-heavy offense in the league (pass rate over expected 6.9, 1st) facing one of the most run-heavy. The Bengals' defense gets after the quarterback, 4th in pressure rate and 3rd in sack rate, but it's soft against the run (28th in rush EPA allowed, 30th in explosive runs allowed), misses tackles and gives up a lot on short throws and third downs. Baltimore's offense is built to attack exactly those weaknesses. The Ravens' risk is on the other side, where the Bengals' volume passing meets a defense that struggles with No. 1 receivers and deep balls. The Book has Baltimore -2.5 at home with a 51.5 total, which reads as a shootout between near-equals.

Availability drives this game. Jackson is day-to-day with an ankle sprain and could practice this week. Jurgens is out, which puts a new center in front of whichever QB starts against a top-five pass rush. Bateman is questionable but expected to be fine, and backup tight end Matt Hibner, guard Andrew Vorhees and rotational DT Broderick Washington Jr. are out. Burrow has started every game for Cincinnati, whose report is light: tight end Tanner Hudson is on IR, and safety Kyle Dugger and receiver Colbie Young, both part-time players, are questionable.

waysToWin.title: Feed Henry into a soft front
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati ranks 28th in rush EPA allowed, 30th in explosive runs allowed and 27th in missed tackles, and Baltimore is 4th in yards per carry. A heavy dose of Henry keeps Burrow on the sideline, controls the clock (the Ravens are 9th in time of possession) and works with Jackson or Huntley. It's the most reliable edge on the board.

waysToWin.title: Andrews and the short game
waysToWin.body: The Bengals give up the 29th-ranked EPA on short passes and are 30th at holding lead tight ends to their usual output, with offenses sending them an above-average share of targets. Mark Andrews, second on the team in targets, and quick throws can beat the pass rush and keep third downs short, where Cincinnati ranks 29th.

waysToWin.title: Make Burrow work underneath
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati gets the ball out quickly, which neutralizes a Ravens pass rush that doesn't get home anyway. But quick throws run into Baltimore's strength: 4th in short-pass EPA allowed. If the Ravens keep everything in front of them and win the possession battle, a pass-first offense ends up with fewer drives than it needs.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush meets a reshuffled line
waysToLose.body: Baltimore's line limits pressure (5th) but its quarterbacks take sacks (22nd in sack rate) and hold the ball. Cincinnati is 4th in pressure rate and 3rd in sack rate, and Jurgens is out. Drive-killing sacks, worse if a less-mobile Jackson or Huntley is under center, are the clearest way this goes wrong.

waysToLose.title: Burrow's volume finds the WR1 hole
waysToLose.body: The league's most pass-heavy offense faces a defense that is 31st in EPA a play allowed to No. 1 receivers and 22nd on deep throws. If Cincinnati's top receiver wins downfield, the Ravens' lack of pressure gives them no way to get off the field, and the 51.5 total turns into a race that a run-first offense isn't built for.

waysToLose.title: Stalled red-zone trips and giveaways
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati is 4th in red-zone TD rate allowed and 6th in turnover differential, so it wins by forcing field goals and taking the ball away. Add Baltimore's penalty habit and poor short-yardage conversion, and long drives can end in three points or none. That's how the Ravens lost to New Orleans as big favorites.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jackson practices and starts. With him, Henry against Cincinnati's run defense should decide the game; without him, the new-look interior line against a top-five pass rush probably will.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying profile supports a playoff-caliber team. Net EPA is 5th, the record matches the point differential, and the run game rests on volume and line play rather than game script. What should hold is Henry's production and a top-ten offense when Jackson is healthy. What probably won't improve much without personnel changes is a defense that doesn't pressure or take the ball away. The penalty and special-teams drag is the one area where real gains are possible.

The schedule is front-loaded with danger: Buffalo's top offense next week and Jacksonville after that. Then come soft spots against the Chargers and Bucs, whose offenses rank near the bottom, before a closing run of four division games against Pittsburgh twice, Cleveland and Cincinnati. All three rivals have strong or solid defenses, and the Browns just held this offense to 10 points. The division probably comes down to December. Jackson's health is the biggest single factor, because the Huntley version of this team needs everything to go right on the ground.
swingFactors: Jackson's ankle and how quickly he's back to full mobility
Jurgens' return and cleaner line play on penalties
Whether the defense finds any pass rush or takeaways

confidence.note: Six games, split between two quarterbacks, with a new coach and the starter's return still uncertain.
